title: The Electricity–Credit Nexus
subtitle: When an energy constraint becomes a financing constraint
thesis: Power prices matter for debt capacity through cash flow, hedging and pass-through. Public aggregate observations do not identify a causal electricity–default elasticity.
status: Historical baseline tested · nexus remains a hypothesis
summary: A 226-month Oslo bankruptcy baseline, explicit identification limits and an energy-to-debt-service stress laboratory.
brief: The stable Oslo all-industry series contains 226 monthly observations from January 2008 to October 2026; counts are not default rates.
Across 36 expanding-origin forecasts, the log-AR/seasonal model has MAE 11.80, versus 15.47 for the previous-year month: a 23.7% reduction.
In-sample R² is only 0.079; a useful benchmark forecast does not validate the proposed electricity transmission mechanism.
The supplied Eurostat electricity export covers 2021-S2 to 2026-S1. Ten half-years cannot support a credible multi-lag credit model with structural breaks.
theory: The cash-flow channel

An electricity-price shock first affects the unhedged energy bill. The borrower absorbs only the share that cannot be passed to customers. Lower operating cash flow then competes with interest and principal repayments. Debt capacity depends on that residual exposure, rather than the headline spot price.
The physical channel

A connection delay or curtailment can reduce output even under a fixed-price contract. Contract tenor, counterparty strength, curtailment rights and local network availability therefore belong in underwriting. ENTSO-E installed capacity and cross-border flows provide system context, not a site-specific guarantee of firm power.
The identification problem

Bankruptcy counts combine firm formation, insolvency rules, sector composition, refinancing conditions and reporting. The regional export uses modern county codes with historical zeros. We select the continuous Oslo geography and all industries, excluding personal-bankruptcy columns and sector subcategories. We do not interpret these observations as a nationwide firm default panel.
decision: High unhedged cost, weak pass-through
Recalculate debt service under a joint price/output shock
Borrower contracts, invoiced MWh, maturities and liquidity
Do not convert the sandbox into PD or an IFRS 9 stage trigger.
Energy-intensive borrower with hedge
Check volume mismatch, collateral calls and hedge expiry
Executed contracts and cash margining terms
Hedge price protection does not establish physical availability.
Data-centre or grid-dependent project
Treat energisation and completion risk explicitly
Connection offer, queue position and milestone covenants
National generation surplus cannot underwrite a local connection.
method: Source: SSB 08551, all industries, total bankruptcies, Oslo code 03. Sort 226 months; do not sum county series with historical zeros. Model log(1+B_t)=a+b log(1+B_(t−1))+c sin(2πm/12)+d cos(2πm/12). Fit by OLS at each expanding origin, forecasting one month ahead over the last 36 months (2023-11–2026-10). Exponentiation gives a conditional-median count forecast, without a lognormal mean correction. Compare against B_(t−12); report MAE/RMSE. Full-sample coefficient intervals use Bartlett Newey–West covariance with 12 lags. No electricity regressor enters this baseline. The sector price scenarios are arithmetic, not estimated PD forecasts.
limits: No firm-level energy exposure, outstanding-credit denominator, borrower failure panel or matched hedge information. Covid-era policy and insolvency changes are potential breaks. Baseline forecast evaluation uses a single holdout; specification selection was not preregistered. No causal or nationwide predictive validation is claimed.
change: A matched firm-level panel linking electricity invoices and contracts to arrears/defaults, with pre-shock exposure and a credible comparison group.
A geography-consistent multi-year price panel and rolling tests showing improvement over rates, sector and macro controls.
Evidence that physical curtailment, rather than energy costs, dominates borrower cash losses.
sensitivity: Electricity-price increase %, holding other assumptions fixed → debt-service coverage
formula:
EBITDA_stress = revenue × margin − revenue × energy_share × price_shock × (1−hedge) × (1−pass_through) − revenue × output_loss × margin.
Debt_service = debt × rate + scheduled_principal.
Coverage = EBITDA_stress / debt_service. This simplified covenant proxy is not cash DSCR: tax, working capital and maintenance capex are excluded.

title: The Economics of Stored Electricity
subtitle: The value of flexibility, after the foresight premium
thesis: Battery economics depend on when energy can be sold and which revenues are executable. Perfect-foresight arbitrage materially overstates the performance of a frozen dispatch rule.
summary: Five Norwegian bidding zones, 43,800 price observations and a chronological storage backtest with explicit cost sensitivities.
brief: At 90% efficiency, NO1’s frozen schedule earns 151.79 NOK per 1 MWh daily charge in the 184-block holdout, before all operating and capital costs.
The same holdout yields a 475.86 NOK/day perfect-foresight upper bound. The frozen rule captures 31.9% of that gross opportunity.
A 2,000-draw circular seven-day block bootstrap puts the NO1 mean between 69.68 and 238.41 NOK/day at the 95% level. This is sampling uncertainty, not a future-return interval.
At 80% efficiency the NO1 fixed-rule mean falls to 66.48 NOK/day. Excluding the final source block changes the 90% result to 153.01.
theory: Storage is a timing asset

The asset buys flexibility between a charging opportunity and a later delivery opportunity. High average prices alone do not guarantee a useful spread. Efficiency losses can make a seemingly attractive pair unprofitable; grid tariffs and throughput costs raise the minimum required spread.
The foresight premium

An optimiser that observes the complete realised day can choose the best charge/discharge pair and avoid bad days. That is an information advantage. Our frozen schedule chooses an ordered pair using only the first 181 blocks, then dispatches unconditionally in the remaining 184. It therefore accepts losses on adverse days instead of silently selecting profitable hindsight trades.
The revenue stack has limits

The workbook includes reserve-market price and volume sheets. They are inventoried, but their revenues are not added to spot arbitrage: qualification, capacity reservation, activation energy, state-of-charge constraints and mutually exclusive commitments would need a joint operational model. NBIM’s November Aypa investment motivates the question; Norwegian prices do not value a North American platform.
decision: Merchant investment
Require a feasible dispatch policy and tariff-inclusive cash flow
Grid agreement, fees, degradation warranty and executable bids
Do not capitalise the perfect-foresight ceiling.
Reserve-led case
Model joint state-of-charge and market commitments
Qualification, activation profile and capacity obligations
Avoid adding incompatible spot and reserve revenues.
Contracted storage
Separate contracted floor from merchant upside
Counterparty credit and availability penalties
A contracted return has a different risk structure.
method: NTNU-hosted Power Market NO 2025 workbook, Strømpris sheet: 8,760 indexed records × five zones. Convert øre/kWh to NOK/MWh by ×10. Partition each zone into 365 sequential 24-index blocks; the workbook lacks timestamp/time-zone columns. Train on blocks 0–180. Evaluate all 276 ordered pairs i<j and choose the pair maximising average 0.9×p_j−p_i in training. Freeze that pair for blocks 181–364. A cycle charges 1 MWh in one hour and delivers 0.9 MWh in a later hour; initial and final state are zero. The hindsight benchmark takes max(0,max_(i<j)(0.9p_j−p_i)); it is an upper bound for this restricted one-cycle model, not all conceivable battery operations. Bootstrap 184 holdout daily outcomes in circular seven-block clusters, 2,000 draws with fixed seed 20261112. Efficiency sensitivity holds the original schedule fixed. NPV repeats the held-out mean as a scenario, applies cost/availability/fade assumptions and discounts annual cash flows.
limits: One year, one chronological split, no seasonal replication. The hosting institution is NTNU; underlying prices are compiled from Nord Pool/Statnett/Norges Bank. The final all-zone zero hour is retained and flagged. The workbook MD5 is checked against the repository record. Exact timestamps and daylight-saving treatment are not authenticated. Reserve sheets and FX are not treated as executable revenue. A 1 MWh charge-equivalent unit is not a fully specified battery procurement quote.
change: A cost-inclusive, timestamp-verified out-of-sample policy with durable positive cash flow over multiple years.
Market saturation or reduced volatility compressing executable spreads.
A credible contracted revenue floor or reserve co-optimisation changing the risk-adjusted result.

inputs.label: Grid / trading fee · NOK per charge

sensitivity: Fee per daily charge · NOK → annual net cash flow · NOK
formula:
Gross frozen spread = efficiency × sale_price − purchase_price.
Annual cash = (mean_spread − fee − degradation) × dispatch_days × availability − fixed_opex.
NPV = −capex + Σ cash_1(1−fade)^(t−1)/(1+discount)^t + residual/(1+discount)^T.
The efficiency response is linear because the schedule is frozen.

title: The Depreciation Illusion
subtitle: Reported earnings and the economics of replacing compute
thesis: Accounting depreciation allocates historical cost. It does not independently measure the replacement cash needed to sustain a competitive AI service.
summary: Six SEC issuer histories with tagged annual cash-flow reconciliation and a transparent replacement-life laboratory.
stats: Oracle CFO less cash investment · USD bn
brief: Oracle’s fiscal year ended 2026-05-31: operating cash flow of 31.977 billion USD and cash PP&E investment of 55.663 billion imply a -23.686 billion cash-flow residual before other investing/financing items.
Microsoft’s fiscal year ended June 2026 and the December-2025 reporters are not a common calendar-year panel; the dashboard preserves fiscal dates.
Amazon and NVIDIA use a productive-assets cash investment tag in recent filings. Tag migrations are resolved by period, never by taking an obsolete tag as current.

A hypothetical 100 billion USD cohort depreciated over six rather than three years changes annual pre-tax expense by 16.667 billion USD at zero salvage. This is arithmetic, not evidence of misstatement.
theory: Three distinct clocks

Book useful life, technological usefulness and cash replacement timing need not coincide. A machine can remain operational while becoming less competitive per unit of energy or inference. Conversely, older equipment can remain profitable in lower-intensity workloads. Replacement schedules require workload and utilisation evidence, not just faster chip release cycles.
Cash investment is not maintenance investment

Total cash capex mixes expansion and replacement. The CFO-minus-cash-investment residual is a disclosed-data reconciliation, not a measure of sustainable free cash flow. Cash flows also reflect working capital and tax timing, and cash capex may omit finance-lease additions. Neither the residual nor a capex/D&A multiple proves overinvestment.
Accounting is not the allegation

The title names an analytical risk: mistaking a cost-allocation estimate for economic durability. Company Facts do not supply enough cohort-level evidence to estimate economic useful lives or conclude that reported depreciation is inappropriate. Audited notes, estimate changes, residual values and impairment disclosures would be required for that assessment.
decision: Equity valuation
Separate growth and replacement cash requirements
Asset cohorts, workload economics, lease additions and useful-life notes
Do not treat EBITDA as distributable owner cash.
Credit analysis
Reconcile reported cash capex with total commitments
Debt maturities, finance leases and purchase obligations
A positive net income does not establish self-funded expansion.
Audit planning
Investigate estimate changes and impairment indicators
Documented useful-life reassessments and cash-generating-unit forecasts
The sandbox does not propose a journal entry.
method: Six supplied SEC Company Facts JSON documents. USD units only; filings dated no later than 12 November 2026. Annual cash flows require form 10-K and duration 330–380 days. Deduplicate each issuer/concept/end date using the latest eligible filing and accession, resolving tag migrations separately for each period. Alternative tags are not added. Retain concept, period start/end, filing date and accession. The output is a latest-vintage historical series, not an as-originally-reported point-in-time panel; consequently no pseudo-real-time securities backtest is claimed. CFO, net income and cash investment are annual flows; assets are period-end stock. D&A tags have differing coverage and are shown explicitly. Cohort scenarios use straight-line zero-to-user-defined salvage allocation and an assumed economic replacement horizon. They do not estimate a historical depreciation bias.
limits: No comparable compute-only asset cohort panel, maintenance-capex split, chip utilisation, lease-adjusted total investment or independent resale data. Issuer fiscal calendars differ. SEC taxonomy does not establish that all capex serves AI. No regression estimates an economic useful life. Accounting or valuation conclusions require the underlying audited notes.
change: Cohort-level evidence that older compute generates sufficient net cash after energy costs for longer than the assumed replacement horizon.
Verified workload migration, resale or retirement data showing consistently shorter economic lives.
Reconciled lease additions and maintenance investment materially changing the apparent funding gap.
sensitivity: Assumed replacement horizon · years → annual after-tax gap · USD billion
formula:
Compute cohort = total cohort × compute share.
Annual book allocation = (compute cohort − salvage) / book life.
Annual economic replacement proxy = (compute cohort − salvage) / replacement horizon.
After-tax gap = (replacement proxy − book allocation) × (1−effective tax).
This is a user-defined cohort scenario, not a company earnings restatement.

title: The Hidden Concentration of Global Capital
subtitle: Many securities, fewer independent economic exposures
thesis: Legal-entity diversification can coexist with common dependence on AI spending, semiconductors, regulation and power. Holdings reveal concentration; they do not by themselves identify factor betas.
summary: NBIM issuer concentration, cross-asset watchlists and corrected real-asset aggregation at the June 2026 snapshot.
brief: The disclosed equity file sums to NOK 16.435 trillion across 7,077 issuer names; the largest ten represent 20.88%.
Issuer HHI is 0.006514; its reciprocal is 153.52. This is an equal-weight concentration equivalent, not a count of statistically independent risks.
The selected Microsoft/Alphabet/Amazon/Meta/NVIDIA/Oracle watchlist represents 12.02% of disclosed equities; matching debt holdings are displayed separately.
Country totals repeated across real-asset rows must be counted once per country. Corrected totals are NOK 371.201 billion for real estate and 83.383 billion for infrastructure.
theory: Concentration is not correlation

HHI answers how uneven portfolio weights are across issuer names. A covariance model answers how returns may co-move. Firms from different sectors can share customers and investment cycles, while one firm can have diversified cash flows. We report the former and present common-factor transmission as a hypothesis.
A common capex cycle

Cloud platforms buy compute; chip designers depend on customer investment; utilities and storage developers supply power and flexibility. A productivity disappointment may affect several links, but in different directions and with different timing. A utility under a long-term contract is not equivalent to an exposed semiconductor supplier.
The time boundary matters

The holdings snapshot is 30 June 2026. NBIM’s 4 November disclosure of a 10% Aypa interest for USD 300 million is a later public event and is discussed separately. It is not inserted into the June holdings or treated as a June observation. The scenario here is not a replication of NBIM’s portfolio stress engine.
decision: Portfolio construction
Map revenue dependencies in addition to sector labels
Issuer exposures, supplier/customer relationships, contract structures
Do not infer full diversification from issuer count.
Risk oversight
Stress selected equity and credit sleeves jointly
Explicit shock magnitudes, duration and exposure weights
Deterministic losses have no assigned probability.
Infrastructure allocation
Separate market exposure from contracted cash flow
Contract tenor, counterparty and power-market basis risk
June holdings omit later direct investments.
method: NBIM eq_20260630 and fi_20260630, UTF-16 semicolon exports, NOK market values. Aggregate equities by exact issuer Name, compute w_i=value_i/Σvalue, HHI=Σw_i², effective count=1/HHI and top-ten weight. Country and sector breakdowns use disclosed classifications. For six named firms, substring name matches are made separately in equity and fixed income and remain a watchlist, not legal-group consolidation. The re/ri exports repeat Total country value for every underlying property or project; assert within-country uniqueness and sum only first country totals. No property-level market values are invented. The dashboard stress applies a common equity decline to a chosen fraction of the six-firm basket, a separate decline to other equities, and first-order duration/spread shocks to bonds. Correlation is used only in an illustrative variance diagnostic, not to net deterministic stress losses.
limits: Single date; no return panel, factor covariance estimate or global capital census. No cap-weight benchmark data sufficient to measure active risk. Country of listing is not the geographic distribution of revenue. Watchlist name matching can omit financing subsidiaries. Linear duration approximations ignore convexity and optionality.
change: A revenue- and holdings-matched return panel showing low common-factor exposure across the selected firms.
Contract-level infrastructure evidence that substantially buffers the same AI capex shock.
Different current holdings or a complete legal-group consolidation materially changing the watchlist weight.
sensitivity: Selected AI basket equity loss · % → portfolio loss · %
formula:
Equity loss = watchlist_weight × exposed_fraction × basket_shock + remaining_equity_weight × other_equity_shock.
Bond loss ≈ interest_duration × yield_shift_pp + spread_duration × spread_shift_pp.
Portfolio loss = equity_sleeve × equity_loss + bond_sleeve × bond_loss + residual_sleeve × other_asset_loss.
All sleeve and shock percentages are user-defined. No probability or VaR interpretation.

title: Europe’s AI Adoption Paradox
subtitle: Adoption can accelerate before macro productivity responds
thesis: Enterprise adoption and measured productivity describe different objects. The supplied country data cannot establish whether AI has delivered a causal macroeconomic dividend.
status: EU27 association · HC3 intervals · temporal holdout
summary: Enterprise AI adoption, firm-size gaps and productivity across 27 EU countries, with robust intervals and a genuine year holdout.
brief: EU adoption among enterprises with at least ten employees rises from 8.06% in 2023 to 19.95% in 2025, a gain of 11.89 percentage points.
For 2025, adoption is 17.00% among small enterprises, 30.36% among medium enterprises and 55.03% among large enterprises in the supplied Eurostat export.
Across 27 EU countries, a one-point higher 2024 adoption share is associated with -0.0171 percentage points of 2025 productivity-per-hour growth; the HC3 95% interval is [-0.0845, 0.0503].
A model trained on 2023 adoption and 2024 growth has 2025 holdout RMSE 1.619 pp, against 1.624 for a training-period mean forecast. This offers little predictive discrimination.
theory: The diffusion lag

Organisational redesign, data quality and complementary investment can delay measurable gains after software adoption. A survey recording any use of AI does not measure intensity, implementation success or value added. Adoption is a diffusion indicator; the productivity outcome still has to be measured.
The aggregation gap

The enterprise survey excludes microbusinesses below ten employees and covers a defined non-financial business population. The national-accounts productivity measure covers a broader economy and is affected by sector mix, capital intensity, hours worked and multinational accounting. A country scatter plot cannot isolate the performance of actual adopting firms.
The European question

Tangen’s conversation with Eric Schmidt frames Europe’s strategic challenge. Our empirical question is narrower: does lagged reported adoption help explain the next year’s country productivity growth? The weak association is compatible with delayed gains, measurement error or confounding. It does not prove that regulation caused a shortfall, or that AI lacks economic value.
decision: Corporate investment
Measure workflow-level unit economics and implementation costs
Before/after outputs, quality, staff time and a comparison group
Survey adoption is not an ROI measure.
Macro strategy
Treat productivity upside as a conditional scenario
National accounts revisions, diffusion intensity and capital deepening
Do not translate adoption shares mechanically into GDP.
Public policy
Test barriers and complementary skills separately
Firm-level panels and evaluation designs
This cross-section cannot rank regulatory regimes causally.
method: Eurostat isoc_eb_ai Sheet 9: enterprises with 10+ employees using at least one AI technology, percentage, annual observations 2021/2023/2024/2025. Size comparison uses Sheets 1, 13 and 17; SMEs are not added to their component size classes. Productivity is nama_10_lp_ulc Sheet 2: real labour productivity per hour, index 2015=100. Join exact country labels for 27 EU members; exclude EU/euro-area aggregates, non-EU states and missing pairs. Growth_2025=100×(index_2025/index_2024−1). Estimate unweighted OLS growth_2025=a+b adoption_2024 with HC3 covariance and asymptotic normal 95% intervals. Check Spearman rank association and leave-one-country-out slopes. Temporal holdout: estimate 2024 growth on 2023 adoption, freeze coefficients, predict 2025 growth from 2024 adoption; compare RMSE with the 2024 cross-country mean. Countries are not assumed independent experimental units; HC3 addresses heteroskedasticity, not regional spillovers. Flags are retained in downloadable normalized files.
limits: Only a few adoption survey waves; no causal identification or long-run panel. Macro productivity and enterprise-survey populations differ. Small n, revisions, country outliers and cross-country dependence limit inference. One held-out year is not evidence of durable forecasting power. No “no effect” conclusion follows from a large p-value.
change: Matched firm-level evidence with credible controls demonstrating persistent productivity gains net of implementation costs.
Several additional survey waves showing stable out-of-sample improvement over sector/macro baselines.
Revisions or intensity-weighted adoption measures changing the cross-country relationship.
sensitivity: Enterprise adoption · % → net productivity contribution · pp
formula:
Gross contribution_pp = adoption_fraction × task_fraction × utilisation_fraction × task_uplift_pct × (1−leakage) × (1−displacement).
Net contribution_pp = gross contribution_pp − implementation_drag_pp.
This is a transparent scenario accounting identity, not a regression forecast or GDP projection.

title: Who Captures the AI Energy Dividend?
subtitle: Electricity rents, public ownership and fiscal incidence
thesis: A larger energy bill is not automatically a public dividend. Public capture depends on incremental profits, effective taxation, ownership, investment costs and who ultimately bears them.
status: Fiscal and energy history · incidence scenarios
summary: Thirty years of Norwegian fiscal accounts, 36 years of electricity balances and a transparent public-capture scenario model.
brief: Consolidated general-government revenue in 2024 is NOK 3203.407 billion; expenditure is 2524.615 billion and net lending is 678.792 billion.
Aggregate 2024 dividends are NOK 403.313 billion. This national-accounts category is not an estimate of AI or electricity-sector dividends.
The 2025 electricity balance records 160,454 GWh primary electricity production, 11,515 GWh imports and 34,315 GWh exports. Net exports are 22,800 GWh.
A hypothetical 100 MW load at 90% utilisation consumes 788.4 GWh annually. Allocation of its fiscal surplus requires assumptions about prices, costs, ownership and public support.
theory: Follow the incidence

An electricity payment moves money from a buyer to suppliers; it is not itself new national income. The relevant increment is producer surplus and other value added after opportunity costs. Taxes and publicly owned company dividends can transfer part of that surplus to government, while higher consumer costs or grid subsidies can offset the benefit.
Ownership changes capture

Public ownership can create a dividend channel after company tax, but it also exposes the public balance sheet to capital costs and risk. The scenario applies an assumed effective tax to incremental profit, then public ownership to after-tax earnings, avoiding a double count. This is a stylised waterfall, not a statutory tax model.
Fiscal history is context

The supplied fiscal series includes petroleum revenues, financial income and other activity unrelated to AI. Electricity balance history establishes physical scale, not a causal relation with budget outcomes. Norwegian energy abundance also does not establish deliverable capacity at a specific data-centre location.
decision: Government budgeting
Require net incremental capture after public costs
Tax base, ownership, subsidy commitments and grid cost allocation
Do not earmark gross electricity sales as fiscal revenue.
Project assessment
Compare with the counterfactual use of scarce power
Alternative demand, export value and local capacity
A new load can redistribute existing rents.
Public investment
Separate commercial return from tax receipts
Capital contributions, downside exposure and dividend policy
Avoid treating public equity capital as free finance.
method: SSB 10721 consolidated General government, 1995–2024. Convert NOK million to NOK billion by ÷1,000. Do not add central and local government totals because intergovernmental flows require consolidation. Reconcile revenue minus total expenditure to net lending within a one-million-NOK rounding tolerance; seven historical years differ by one source unit. SSB 11561, Electricity product, GWh, 1990–2025; retain production, imports, exports, final consumption and distribution losses as distinct balance items. PJ columns are not mixed with GWh; energy-conversion and own-use components are not silently omitted from a claimed full balance identity. ENTSO-E load, domestic production, flows, installed generation and transmission inventory provide a 2025/first-half-2026 system cross-check; missing transmission measures remain missing. The supplied quarterly fiscal summary is excluded because its label and magnitudes are inconsistent; no undocumented ×1,000 correction is made. No historical AI fiscal multiplier is estimated: incremental AI-linked receipts and a credible counterfactual are absent. The forward model is an incidence waterfall, not an econometric projection.
limits: No AI-specific tax receipts, public utility profit bridge, marginal generation costs, spatial grid constraints or verified counterfactual power demand. Effective tax and dividend payout are scenario assumptions. Fiscal observations end in 2024; more recent power observations do not extend fiscal history. The aggregate non-petroleum resource-tax line is not treated as total electricity taxation.
change: Audited incremental project-level tax, dividend and subsidy accounts establishing positive net public capture.
Evidence that grid expansion or foregone alternative uses absorb most of the incremental surplus.
Firm contracted load, power and ownership data replacing the stylised incidence assumptions.

inputs.label: Annual public grid cost · NOK million

sensitivity: Electricity price · NOK/MWh → annual net public capture · NOK bn
formula:
GWh = MW × 8,760 × load_factor / 1,000.
Revenue_NOK_bn = GWh × price_NOK_MWh / 1,000,000.
Profit = revenue × margin; tax = profit × effective_tax.
Public dividend = (profit−tax) × public_ownership_capture.
Net public capture = (tax + dividend − public_subsidy − public_grid_cost) × (1−leakage).
The public ownership control incorporates the assumed dividend payout ratio.
